title: Deuterium and Oxygen-17 Metabolic Imaging
summary: Deuterium metabolic imaging works because the background is almost empty and the relaxation is almost free. 2H sits at 0.0115 to 0.0156 percent natural abundance, so the only resting peak is HDO at roughly 9 to 13 mM, and after oral [6,6-2H2]glucose the glucose, Glx and lactate peaks rise out of near zero with no water or lipid suppression needed. The per-nucleus sensitivity is only 9.65e-3 of 1H, but a 70 ms glucose T1 and a 330 to 360 ms water T1 let you run TR at 250 ms and average hard, which recovers a large part of the gamma penalty; the price is a working spectrum only 3.5 ppm wide, 160 Hz at 7T and 69 Hz at 3T, so the shim and the fit carry the experiment. 17O is the mirror case: a 20 mM natural abundance H2-17O background that you must detect a 5 to 7 percent increase on top of, a 1.8 to 3 ms T2* that forces UTE radial readouts and hundred-Hz linewidths, and a gas cost so high that cohorts are five subjects and the breathing circuit exists to recycle exhaled gas.

facts.label: 2H nucleus and Larmor frequencies
facts.value: Spin 1, gyromagnetic ratio 6.536 MHz/T (gamma = 4.1066e7 rad/s/T), electric quadrupole moment 2.86 mb. 19.6 MHz at 3T, 45.7 MHz at 7T, 61.4 MHz at 9.4T. Sensitivity per nucleus at fixed field is 9.65e-3 of 1H; at natural abundance the receptivity is about 1.1e-6 of 1H
facts.note: Note that the 6.5-fold lower gamma does NOT change the gradient needed for a slice of given thickness at a bandwidth fixed in ppm: gamma cancels, since both the offset per ppm and the gradient-induced spread scale with it. What it costs you is bandwidth in hertz. A pulse of fixed duration covers the same hertz for 2H as for 1H, and that is 6.5 times more ppm, so chemical shift displacement is small while the gradient amplitude for a given slice is unchanged.

facts.label: Natural abundance 2H background
facts.value: Tabulated natural abundance ranges from 0.0115 percent (fresh water, temperate) to 0.0156 percent (standard mean ocean water). In human brain this gives a resting HDO peak of 8.96 +/- 0.7 mM measured directly at 7T (range 7.5 to 10.1 mM); theory spans 8.9 mM (0.0115 percent, 70 percent brain water) to 13.7 mM (0.0156 percent, 80 percent water). Older DMI papers assumed 10.1 to 17.8 mM
facts.note: This is a genuine range, not a constant: deuterium in tap water varies by about 15 percent across the USA, so an assumed value biases every concentration referenced to it.

facts.label: 2H relaxation in human brain at 7T
facts.value: Natural abundance HDO T1 = 358 +/- 21 ms in gray matter and 328 +/- 12 ms in white matter, unlocalized 335 +/- 6 ms; HDO T2 = 36 +/- 2 / 34 +/- 2 ms (GM/WM), unlocalized 31 +/- 2 ms. 2H glucose T1 = 70 +/- 5 / 73 +/- 4 ms, T2 = 36 +/- 1 / 34 +/- 2 ms. 2H Glx T1 = 172 +/- 15 / 172 +/- 12 ms, T2 = 37 +/- 2 / 35 +/- 2 ms
facts.note: 2H relaxation is quadrupolar and largely field independent, so the 4T values run close to these rather than far from them, and where they differ they are slightly shorter, not longer (HDO near 320 ms GM and 290 ms WM, glucose near 64 to 67 ms, Glx near 139 to 146 ms, lactate near 297 ms); quote the field with the number anyway.

facts.label: What the short T1 buys you
facts.value: At TR = 250 ms, TR/T1 is 3.6 for 2H glucose (Ernst angle 88 degrees, essentially fully relaxed) but only 0.74 for HDO (Ernst angle 61 degrees). A 5 min DMI time point at 7T is roughly 1200 excitations
facts.note: Partial saturation of the water peak at short TR is a feature, not a bug: it suppresses the one resonance that would otherwise dominate the spectrum while leaving the metabolites unweighted.

facts.label: Chemical shifts and the usable spectral width
facts.value: HDO 4.8 ppm, glucose 3.8 to 3.9 ppm, Glx 2.35 to 2.4 ppm, lactate CH3 and lipid CH2 both near 1.3 ppm. The 2H ppm scale is the same as 1H (nominally 0 to 12 ppm for organics, 548 Hz at 7T and 235 Hz at 3T), but the whole in vivo DMI spectrum lives in 3.5 ppm: 160 Hz at 7T, 69 Hz at 3T. Measured in vivo 2H linewidths at 7T are 11 to 26 Hz FWHM
facts.note: The water to glucose gap is 0.9 to 1.0 ppm, which is 41 to 46 Hz at 7T but only 18 to 20 Hz at 3T, so at clinical field the separation is barely larger than the line itself.

facts.label: Dose, route and timing
facts.value: Oral [6,6-2H2]glucose at 0.25 to 0.80 g/kg body weight in 150 to 300 mL water, capped at 60 g, after a fast of 4 h or more. Plasma glucose and 2H atom-percent excess rise over the first 40 min then plateau. 0.50 g/kg gives comparable and well detectable brain glucose and Glx signals to 0.75 g/kg at 7T. Brain Glx reaches 1.29 +/- 0.15 mM (GM) and 1.10 +/- 0.13 mM (WM) one hour after ingestion
facts.note: Dose above 0.50 g/kg mostly buys plasma glucose, not brain Glx, and raises the osmotic and nausea burden; intravenous infusion gives cleaner kinetics but loses the simplicity that makes DMI attractive.

facts.label: Labeling rates and the Glx versus lactate readout
facts.value: In healthy brain at 7T, d[Glx]/dt = 9.2 umol/L/min (SE 0.44 to 0.61) and d[Lac]/dt = 0.5 umol/L/min. In treatment-naive glioblastoma, tumor d[Glx]/dt falls to 3.8 umol/L/min and d[Lac]/dt rises to 2.3 umol/L/min; mean tumor concentrations near 0.5 +/- 0.2 mM for both Glx and lactate at the last time point
facts.note: In healthy brain 2H lactate is usually below the detection limit, so a visible lactate peak is either pathology or an artifact; the Lac/(Lac+Glx) ratio is the quantity that separates glycolytic from oxidative tissue.

facts.label: DMI voxel volume versus field
facts.value: Reported nominal voxel volumes in human brain: 14 to 33 mL at 3T; 8 mL at 4T (1 mL with reduced FOV); 2 mL at 7T (1 mL reduced FOV, 6.9 mL for whole-brain UTE-CSI); down to 0.75 mL at 7T with concentric ring trajectories plus denoising. Acquisition 5 to 30 min per time point, and 10 min or better temporal resolution is needed to follow the kinetics
facts.note: Going 3T to 7T is worth roughly a factor of 3 to 4 in SNR, more than the bare 2.3-fold ratio of the fields, which is why almost all quantitative human DMI is done at 7T or above.

facts.label: Comparison with FDG-PET
facts.value: A 370 MBq 18F-FDG study delivers about 7.0 mSv effective dose (ICRP 128 coefficient 0.019 mSv/MBq) at 3 to 6 mm FWHM spatial resolution and picomolar tracer sensitivity; 18F half-life 110 min means no significant label at 24 h. DMI delivers zero ionizing dose at 1 to 7 mL voxels and millimolar sensitivity
facts.note: The trade is resolution and sensitivity against specificity and repeatability: FDG is trapped as FDG-6-phosphate and reports uptake only, whereas DMI separates glucose, Glx and lactate and can be repeated without a dose budget.

facts.label: 17O nucleus and its 20 mM background
facts.value: Spin 5/2, gyromagnetic ratio 5.774 MHz/T (negative), quadrupole moment about -25.6 mb, natural abundance 0.037 to 0.038 percent. 17.3 MHz at 3T, 40.4 MHz at 7T. Sensitivity per nucleus is 2.91e-2 of 1H, receptivity at natural abundance about 1.1e-5. Natural abundance H2-17O is 20.56 umol per gram of water, so roughly 15 to 17 mM in tissue after the water fraction
facts.note: Unlike 2H there is no free background: the baseline is large, and the entire 17O2 inhalation experiment is a 7.3 percent (gray matter) to 5 percent (white matter) signal increase on top of it.

facts.label: 17O relaxation and linewidth
facts.value: Quadrupolar relaxation in the extreme narrowing limit, so essentially field independent. In vivo rat brain at 16.4T: T1 = 6.84 +/- 0.67 ms, T2* = 1.77 +/- 0.04 ms. Human brain 17O T2* is taken as 2 to 3 ms; T1 is under 5 ms at 9.4T. The 17O quadrupolar time constant for water in vivo is about 4.47 +/- 0.14 ms
facts.note: T2* of 2 ms is a linewidth near 160 Hz, or 4 ppm at 7T, so 17O is an imaging nucleus and not a spectroscopy nucleus; TE must be well under 1 ms, which means radial UTE (TE 0.51 to 0.56 ms) and nothing with a spin echo in it.

facts.label: CMRO2 by direct 17O
facts.value: Human brain at 3T with 8 mm nominal isotropic resolution: 1.45 +/- 0.20 umol/g/min in gray matter and 0.95 +/- 0.11 umol/g/min in white matter; regionally 1.39 (frontal), 1.44 (parietal), 1.54 (occipital GM), 1.20 thalamus, 1.24 insula, 1.54 cerebellum. Anesthetized rat brain at 9.4T: 2.19 +/- 0.14 umol/g/min
facts.note: Inhaled 17O2 is MR invisible as gas and when bound to hemoglobin, so any signal rise is metabolically generated H2-17O; that is the whole basis of the measurement and the reason it is a true CMRO2 and not an oxygenation proxy.

facts.label: 17O gas: what an exam actually consumes
facts.value: Human protocols use 70 percent enriched 17O2, about 2.5 L at STP per subject, delivered in 50 mL pulses by a demand oxygen delivery system triggered on inspiration, followed by a rebreathing circuit with a CO2 absorber to reclaim the exhaled fraction. Inhalation lasts 9 to 12 min, total acquisition 40 to 46 min. Published cohorts are typically 5 subjects, limited explicitly by gas cost. For reference, 70 percent enriched H2-17O water (38.4 M) was quoted at close to 900 EUR/mL
facts.note: The pulsed-demand delivery and rebreathing hardware exist for no reason other than to conserve gas; budget the isotope before you budget the scanner time.

facts.label: Indirect 17O detection via 1H T2
facts.value: 1H-17O scalar coupling is J = 91 to 92.5 Hz, shortening water 1H T2 by scalar relaxation of the second kind modulated by proton exchange. At natural abundance the effect is negligible: the calibration below gives an 17O-dependent term of 0.405 x 0.037 = 0.015 s^-1, well under a hundredth of a hertz of linewidth, which is why the indirect method needs enrichment to work at all. At 3T the 1H R2 rises linearly with enrichment as R2 = 0.405 * C + 0.3215 s^-1 for C in atom percent, usable from about 0.25 to 5.5 percent; R1 and R2* show no significant response
facts.note: The 0.25 percent floor is roughly 7 times natural abundance, which is why indirect detection is practical for injected H2-17O boluses but marginal for the few percent enrichment that 17O2 metabolism actually produces.

practice: Run DMI with TR between 200 and 300 ms and a flip near the water Ernst angle (about 60 degrees at TR 250 ms, T1 340 ms). Glucose and Glx are effectively fully relaxed at that TR, so no saturation correction is needed for them while the water peak is usefully attenuated.

Acquire a pre-ingestion baseline DMI scan whenever the clinical schedule allows. It gives you the subject's own natural abundance HDO as an internal concentration reference and a per-voxel receive-sensitivity correction, and it is the only way to know the real starting point for the water peak.

Do not trust a tabulated natural abundance value for absolute quantification. Deuterium in drinking water varies about 15 percent nationally and about 5 percent within a single county, and brain water fraction runs 70 to 80 percent. If the number matters, take a baseline blood sample and measure plasma HDO by mass spectrometry.

Shim on 1H with the vendor routine, then check that the HDO linewidth is in the 11 to 26 Hz range before you start the clock. At 3T, where glucose sits only 18 to 20 Hz from water, a frontal-lobe shim failure merges the two peaks and the fit will silently allocate the area to whichever basis function wins.

For 17O use a 3D radial or spiral UTE readout with TE at or below 0.55 ms, TR 7 to 10 ms, an RF pulse of 0.8 to 0.9 ms and a flip angle near the Ernst optimum, about 80 degrees at TR 7 to 10 ms when T1 is under 5 ms; SAR at 17 MHz is not what limits you, and golden-angle ordering so you can reconstruct with a sliding window at 1 min temporal resolution after the fact.

Budget 17O ROIs by voxel count, not by anatomy. At 8 mm nominal resolution a gray matter region needs at least 25 voxels and white matter at least 50 to hold the CMRO2 fit error inside 5 percent; smaller structures will be noise-limited before they are partial-volume-limited.

Watch the RF environment at 19.6 and 45.7 MHz. One 7T group had to kill the technical-room lighting at the circuit breaker to drop the noise floor on the 2H channel, and DMI at 3T needed modified gradient-line filters (eightfold larger capacitors, split cores for differential filtering) because the vendor filters leak at the 2H frequency; unfiltered, spectral SNR dropped by up to 25-fold.
pitfalls: The rising HDO peak is not local metabolism. Metabolically produced HDO equilibrates across the whole body and washes into the voxel from everywhere, including into CSF, so a bright central HDO region can be read as basal ganglia glucose consumption when it is partly just water. Treat HDO as a reference and a whole-body integral, and put the local metabolic claim on Glx and lactate.

The peripheral ring of apparent lactate is subcutaneous lipid. Lipid CH2 and lactate CH3 both sit at 1.3 ppm and 2H is not immune to lipid contamination just because the spectrum is sparse; any lactate map should be checked against the skull outline before it is believed.

Deuterium label does not clear like 18F. HDO persists for days, so a same-day or same-week repeat starts from an elevated and unknown baseline, and the natural abundance internal reference is no longer natural abundance. FDG-PET has no significant label left at 24 h; DMI does.

17O CMRO2 in white matter is systematically overestimated, by 32 to 48 percent against PET at 8 mm resolution, because of partial volume mixing with gray matter and CSF. Deep gray structures go the other way and read 8 to 39 percent low. Partial volume correction is not optional at clinical field.

Indirect 17O via 1H R2 depends on proton exchange, so it is sensitive to pH and temperature, not just to 17O concentration. Normalizing to the pre-contrast R2 removes most of the bias, but absolute enrichment from a single R2 measurement will be wrong in tissue where pH differs from the calibration phantom.

Fitting a 3.5 ppm wide spectrum at 3T with 20 Hz peak separations makes the result a property of the basis set and the prior constraints as much as of the data. Report Cramer-Rao lower bounds, mask on them (30 percent is a common threshold, and it can discard 31 to 58 percent of voxels), and do not report ratios where numerator and denominator both approach zero.
